{{Short description|Mathematical operation}}
{{more footnotes needed|date=April 2020}}
In [[analytic number theory]], a [[Dirichlet series]], or [[Dirichlet generating function]] (DGF), of a sequence is a common way of understanding and summing [[arithmetic functions]] in a meaningful way. A little known, or at least often forgotten about, way of expressing formulas for arithmetic functions and their [[summatory function]]s is to perform an [[integral transform]] that inverts the operation of forming the DGF of a sequence. This inversion is analogous to performing an [[Z-transform#Inverse Z-transform|inverse Z-transform]] to the [[generating function]] of a sequence to express formulas for the series coefficients of a given ordinary generating function.

For now, we will use this page as a compendium of "oddities" and oft-forgotten facts about transforming and inverting Dirichlet series, DGFs, and relating the inversion of a DGF of a sequence to the sequence's summatory function. We also use the notation for coefficient extraction usually applied to formal [[generating functions]] in some complex variable, by denoting <math>[n^{-s}] D_f(s) =: f(n)</math> for any positive integer <math>n \geq 1</math>, whenever

:<math>D_f(s) := \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{f(n)}{n^s}, \quad \Re(s) > \sigma_{0,f},</math>

denotes the DGF (or [[Dirichlet series]]) of ''f'' which is taken to be [[Absolute convergence|absolutely convergent]] whenever the [[real part]] of ''s'' is greater than the [[abscissa of convergence|abscissa of absolute convergence]], <math>\sigma_{0,f} \in \mathbb{R}</math>.

The relation of the [[Mellin transformation]] of the summatory function of a sequence to the DGF of a sequence provides us with a way of expressing arithmetic functions <math>f(n)</math> such that <math>f(1) \neq 0</math>, and the corresponding [[Dirichlet inverse]] functions, <math>f^{-1}(n)</math>, by inversion formulas involving the summatory function, defined by

:<math>S_f(x) := {\sum_{n \leq x}}^\prime f(n), \quad \forall x \geq 1.</math>

In particular, provided that the DGF of some arithmetic function ''f'' has an [[Analytic continuation#Example II: An interpretation of F as the summatory function for some arithmetic sequence|analytic continuation]] to <math>s \mapsto -s</math>, we can express the [[Mellin transform]] of the summatory function of ''f'' by the continued DGF formula as

:<math>\mathcal{M}[S_f](s) = -\frac{D_f(-s)}{s}.</math>

It is often also convenient to express formulas for the summatory functions over the [[Dirichlet inverse]] function of ''f'' using this construction of a Mellin inversion type problem.

==Preliminaries: Notation, conventions and known results on DGFs==

===DGFs for Dirichlet inverse functions===

Recall that an arithmetic function is Dirichlet invertible, or has an inverse <math>f^{-1}(n)</math> with respect to [[Dirichlet convolution]] such that <math>(f \ast f^{-1})(n) = \delta_{n,1}</math>, or equivalently <math>f \ast f^{-1} = \mu \ast 1 \equiv \varepsilon</math>, if and only if <math>f(1) \neq 0</math>. It is not difficult to prove that if <math>D_f(s)</math> is the DGF of ''f'' and is absolutely convergent for all complex ''s'' satisfying <math>\Re(s) > \sigma_{0,f}</math>, then the DGF of the Dirichlet inverse is given by <math>D_{f^{-1}}(s) = 1 / D_f(s)</math> and is also absolutely convergent for all <math>\Re(s) > \sigma_{0,f}</math>. The positive real <math>\sigma_{0,f}</math> associated with each invertible arithmetic function ''f'' is called the [[abscissa of convergence]].

We also see the following identities related to the [[Dirichlet inverse]] of some function ''g'' that does not vanish at one:

:<math>\begin{align}(g^{-1} \ast \mu)(n) & = [n^{-s}]\left(\frac{1}{\zeta(s) D_g(s)}\right) \\ (g^{-1} \ast 1)(n) & = [n^{-s}]\left(\frac{\zeta(s)}{D_g(s)}\right).\end{align}</math>

===Summatory functions===

Using the same convention in expressing the result of [[Perron formula|Perron's formula]], we assume that the summatory function of a (Dirichlet invertible) arithmetic function <math>f</math>, is defined for all real <math>x \geq 0</math> according to the formula

:<math>S_f(x) := {\sum_{n \leq x}}^{\prime} f(n) = \begin{cases} 0, & 0 \leq x < 1 \\ \sum\limits_{n < [x]} f(n), & x \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Z}^{+} \wedge x \geq 1 \\ \sum\limits_{n \leq [x]} f(n) - \frac{f(x)}{2}, & x \in \mathbb{Z}^{+}. \end{cases}</math>

We know the following relation between the [[Mellin transform]] of the summatory function of ''f'' and the DGF of ''f'' whenever <math>\Re(s) > \sigma_{0,f}</math>:

:<math>D_f(s) = s \cdot \int_1^{\infty} \frac{S_f(x)}{x^{s+1}} dx.</math>

Some examples of this relation include the following identities involving the [[Mertens function]], or summatory function of the [[Moebius function]], the [[prime zeta function]] and the [[prime-counting function]], and the Riemann [[prime-counting function]]:

:<math>\begin{align}\frac{1}{\zeta(s)} & = s \cdot \int_1^{\infty} \frac{M(x)}{x^{s+1}} dx \\ P(s) & = s \cdot \int_1^{\infty} \frac{\pi(x)}{x^{s+1}} dx \\ \log \zeta(s) & = s \cdot \int_0^{\infty} \frac{\Pi_0(x)}{x^{s+1}} dx.\end{align}</math>

==Statements of the integral formula for Dirichlet inversion==

===Classical integral formula===

For any ''s'' such that <math>\sigma := \Re(s) > \sigma_{0,f}</math>, we have that

:<math>f(x) \equiv [x^{-s}] D_f(s) = \lim_{T \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{2T} \int_{-T}^T x^{\sigma+\imath t} D_f(\sigma+\imath t) \, dt.</math>

If we write the DGF of ''f'' according to the [[Mellin transform]] formula of the summatory function of ''f'', then the stated integral formula simply corresponds to a special case of [[Perron's formula]]. Another variant of the previous formula stated in Apostol's book provides an integral formula for an alternate sum in the following form for <math>c,x > 0</math> and any real <math>\sigma > \sigma_{0,f}-c</math> where we denote <math>\Re(s) := \sigma</math>:

:<math>{\sum_{n \leq x}}^{\prime} \frac{f(n)}{n^s} = \frac{1}{2\pi\imath} \int_{c-\imath\infty}^{c+\imath\infty} D_f(s+z) \frac{x^z}{z} dz.</math>

====Direct proof: from Apostol's book====

# Define the Dirichlet series <math display="inline">f(s) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n n^{-s}</math> and its associated partial sums <math display="inline">F(x) = \sum_{n=1}^x a_n</math>.
# Define the function <math display="inline">g(x) = \sum_{n=1}^x a_n \lfloor x/n \rfloor</math>.
# Use partial summation to write <math display="inline">F(x) = \int_1^x g(t) dt + a_1</math>.
# Apply the [[Euler–Maclaurin formula|Euler–Maclaurin summation formula]] to obtain an approximation for <math display="inline">F(x)</math> in terms of <math display="inline">g(x)</math> and its derivatives.
# Express the error term in the approximation as an integral of a certain function <math display="inline">R(u)</math> over the interval <math display="inline">[1, x]</math>.
# Use [[Abel's summation formula]] to express <math display="inline">g(x)</math> as a sum of integrals involving <math display="inline">f(s)</math> and its derivatives.
# Express the integrals involving <math display="inline">f(s)</math> and its derivatives in terms of <math display="inline">R(u)</math> and its derivatives.
# Substitute the results from steps 4, 5, and 7 into the formula from step 3, and simplify to obtain the classical integral formula for Dirichlet inversion.

This proof shows that the function <math display="inline">f(s)</math> can be recovered from its associated Dirichlet series by means of an integral, which is known as the classical integral formula for Dirichlet inversion.

====Special cases of the formula====

If we are interested in expressing formulas for the [[Dirichlet inverse]] of ''f'', denoted by <math>f^{-1}(n)</math> whenever <math>f(1) \neq 0</math>, we write <math>D_f(s) = 1 + s \cdot A_f(s)</math>. Then we have by absolute convergence of the DGF for any <math>\Re(s) > \sigma_{0,f}</math> that

:<math>\begin{align}\int \frac{x^{\imath t}}{D_f(\sigma+\imath t)} \,dt & = \int \left(\sum_{j \geq 0} (\sigma+\imath t)^{j} \times \sum_{k=0}^{j} (-1)^k D_f(\sigma+\imath t)^k \frac{\log^{j-k}(x)}{(j-k)!}\right) \, dt.\end{align}</math>

Now we can call on [[integration by parts]] to see that if we denote by <math>F^{(-m)}(x) = \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{F^{(n)}(0)}{n!} x^{n+m} \times \frac{n!}{(n+m)!}</math> the <math>m^{th}</math> [[antiderivative]] of ''F'', for any fixed non-negative integers <math>k \geq 0</math>, we have

:<math>\int (ax+b)^k \cdot F(ax+b) \, dx = \sum_{j=0}^{k} \frac{k!}{a \cdot j!} (-1)^{k-j} t^j F^{(j+1-k)}(ax+b).</math>

Thus we obtain that

:<math>\begin{align}\int_{-T}^T \frac{x^{\imath t}}{D_f(\sigma+\imath t)} \, dt & = \frac{1}{\imath} \left(\sum_{j \geq 0} \sum_{k=0}^j \sum_{m=0}^k \frac{k!}{m!} (-1)^m (\sigma+\imath t)^{m} \left[D_f^k\right]^{(j+1-k)}(\sigma+\imath t) \frac{\log^{j-k}(x)}{(j-k)!}\right) \Biggr|_{t=-T}^{t=+T}.\end{align}</math>

We also can relate the iterated integrals for the <math>k^{th}</math> antiderivatives of ''F'' by a finite sum of ''k'' single integrals of power-scaled versions of ''F'':

:<math>F^{(-k)}(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \binom{k-1}{i} \frac{(-1)^i}{(k-1)!} \int \frac{F(x)}{x^i} \, dx.</math>

In light of this expansion, we can then write the partially limiting ''T''-truncated Dirichlet series inversion integrals at hand in the form of

:<math>\begin{align}\frac{1}{2T} \int_{-T}^T \frac{x^{\imath t}}{D_f(\sigma+\imath t)} \, dt & = \frac{1}{2T \cdot \imath} \left(\sum_{j \geq 0} \sum_{k=0}^{j} \sum_{m=0}^k \sum_{n=0}^{j-k} \binom{j-k}{n} \frac{(-1)^{k+n+m} \cdot k!}{(j-k)! \cdot m!} (\sigma+\imath t)^{m} \frac{\log^{j-k}(x)}{(j-k)!} \int_{0}^{\sigma+\imath t} \left[A_f^k\right](v) \frac{dv}{v^n} \right) \Biggr|_{t=-T}^{t=+T} \\ & = \frac{1}{2T \cdot \imath} \left(\sum_{j \geq 0} \sum_{k=0}^{j} \sum_{m=0}^k \frac{(-1)^{j-k} \cdot (-s)^m}{m!} \frac{\log^{k}(x)}{k!} \int_0^1 s \cdot D_f^{j-k}(rs) \left(1-\frac{1}{rs}\right)^k \, dv\right) \Biggr|_{s=\sigma-\imath T}^{s=\sigma+\imath T} \\ & = \frac{s\left(e^{-s}+O_s(1)\right)}{2T  \cdot \imath} \int_0^{1} \frac{x^{1-\frac{1}{rs}}}{1+D_f(rs)} dr \Biggr|_{s=\sigma-\imath T}^{s=\sigma+\imath T} \\ & = \frac{\left(e^{-s}+O_s(1)\right)}{2T \cdot \imath} \int_0^{s} \frac{x^{1-\frac{1}{v}}}{1+D_f(v)} \, dv \Biggr|_{s=\sigma-\imath T}^{s=\sigma+\imath T}.\end{align}</math>

===Statements in the language of Mellin transformations===

* The Dirichlet generating function of a sequence <math>a(n)</math> is the Mellin transform of the sequence, evaluated at <math>s=1</math>: <math display="inline">\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{a_n}{n^s} = \int_0^\infty x^{s-1} \left(\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n e^{-nx}\right) dx = \mathcal{M}{a_n}(s)</math>.
* The Dirichlet inverse of a sequence <math>a(n)</math> is related to the inverse Mellin transform of its generating function: <math display="inline">a_n = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty} \frac{\sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{\mu(m)}{m^{s}}\mathcal{M}{a_n}(s)}{n^s} ds</math>, where <math>c</math> is a [[real number]] greater than the abscissa of convergence of the Dirichlet series <math display="inline">\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n/n^s</math>.
* The Mellin transform of a [[convolution]] of two sequences <math>a(n)</math> and <math>b(n)</math> is the product of their Mellin transforms: <math display="inline">\mathcal{M}{(a*b)_n}(s) = \mathcal{M}{a_n}(s) \mathcal{M}{b_n}(s)</math>.
* If <math>a(n)</math> is a sequence and <math>f(x)</math> is a function such that the integral <math display="inline">\int_0^\infty \frac{f(x)}{x^{s+1}}dx</math> converges absolutely and uniformly for <math>s</math> in some right half plane, then we can define a Dirichlet series by <math display="inline">a_n = \frac{1}{n^s}\int_0^\infty f(x) e^{-nx}dx</math>, and the Dirichlet series is the Mellin transform of <math>f(x)</math>.

===A formal generating-function-like convolution lemma===

Suppose that we wish to treat the integrand integral formula for Dirichlet coefficient inversion in powers of <math>(\imath t)^k</math> where <math>[(\imath t)^{k}] F(\sigma+\imath t) = F^{(k)})(\sigma) / k!</math>, and then proceed as if we were evaluating a traditional integral on the real line. Then we have that

:<math>\begin{align}\hat{D}_f(x; \sigma, T) & := \int_{-T}^T x^{\sigma+\imath t} D_f(\sigma+\imath t)\, dt \\ & = \sum_{m \geq 0} \int_{-T}^{T} x^{\sigma+\imath t} (\imath t)^m \frac{D_f^{(m)}(\sigma)}{m!} \\ & = \sum_{m \geq 0} \int_{-T}^T t^{2m} x^{\sigma+\imath t} \frac{(-1)^m D_f^{(2m)}(\sigma)}{(2m)!}\,dt + \imath \times \sum_{m \geq 0} \int_{-T}^T t^{2m+1} x^{\sigma+\imath t} \frac{(-1)^m A^{(2m+1)}(\sigma)}{(2m+1)!} \,dt.\end{align}</math>

We require the result given by the following formula, which is proved rigorously by an application of [[integration by parts]], for any non-negative integer <math>m \geq 0</math>:

:<math>\begin{align}\hat{I}_m(T) & := \int_{-T}^{T} \frac{(\imath t)^m}{m!} x^{\imath t} \,dt \\ & = \sum_{r=0}^{m} \frac{\left(x^{\imath T} + (-1)^{r+1} x^{-\imath T}\right) (-\imath)^{r+1}}{\log^{k+1-r}(x)} \cdot \frac{T^r}{r!} \\ & = \frac{\cos(T \log x)}{T \log x} \times \sum_{r=0}^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor} \frac{(-1)^{r+1} T^{2r}}{\log^{k-2r}(x) (2r)!} + \frac{\sin(T \log x)}{T \log x} \times \sum_{r=0}^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor} \frac{(-1)^{r+1} T^{2r+1}}{\log^{k-2r-1}(x) (2r+1)!}.\end{align}</math>

So the respective real and imaginary parts of our [[arithmetic function]] coefficients ''f'' at positive integers ''x'' satisfy:

:<math>\begin{align}\operatorname{Re}(f(x)) & = x^{\sigma} \times \lim_{T \rightarrow \infty} \sum_{m \geq 0} D_f^{(2m)}(\sigma) \cdot \frac{\hat{I}_{2m}(T)}{2T} \\ \operatorname{Im}(f(x)) & = x^{\sigma} \times \lim_{T \rightarrow \infty} \sum_{m \geq 0} D_f^{(2m+1)}(\sigma) \cdot \frac{\hat{I}_{2m+1}(T)}{2T}.\end{align}</math>

The last identities suggest an application of the [[Generating function transformation#Hadamard products and diagonal generating functions|Hadamard product]] formula for [[generating function transformation|generating functions]]. In particular, we can work out the following identities which express the real and imaginary parts of our function ''f'' at ''x'' in the following forms:<ref>To apply the [[generating function transformation|integral formula for the Hadamard product]], we observe that

:<math>\begin{align}\sum_{r=0}^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor} \frac{(-1)^{r+1} T^{2r}}{\log^{k-2r}(x) (2r)!} & = -\frac{1}{2}[z^k]\left(\frac{e^{\imath T \sqrt{z}}}{1-\frac{z}{\log x}} + \frac{e^{-\imath T \sqrt{z}}}{1+\frac{z}{\log x}} \right) \\ \sum_{r=0}^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor} \frac{(-1)^{r+1} T^{2r+1}}{\log^{k-2r-1}(x) (2r+1)!} & = -\frac{1}{2}[z^{k}]\left(\frac{e^{\imath T \sqrt{z}}}{1-\frac{z}{\log x}} - \frac{e^{-\imath T \sqrt{z}}}{1+\frac{z}{\log x}} \right).\end{align}</math>

From this observation, the formula stated below is now a standard application of the cited integral formula to compute the Hadamard product of two generating functions. 
</ref>

:<math>\begin{align}\operatorname{Re}(f(x)) & = \lim_{T \rightarrow \infty} \left[\frac{x^{\sigma}}{2T} \times \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \left(D_f(\sigma+\imath T \cdot e^{\imath s}) + D_f(\sigma - \imath T e^{\imath s})\right) \left(FUNC(e^{-\imath s})\right) \, ds\right] \\ 
\operatorname{Im}(f(x)) & = \lim_{T \rightarrow \infty} \left[\frac{x^\sigma}{2T} \times \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi \left(D_f(\sigma+\imath T \cdot e^{\imath s}) - D_f(\sigma - \imath T e^{\imath s}\right) () \, ds \right].\end{align}</math>

Notice that in the special case where the arithmetic function ''f'' is strictly real-valued, we expect that the inner terms in the previous limit formula are always zero (i.e., for any ''T'').
